explain:
A sender instructed a payment of GBP 20,000 with field 71A set to BEN, so the beneficiary would bear every charge. The beneficiary was credited almost in full, and the sender was billed for charges it never agreed to pay.

Somewhere in the chain, a bank copy showed SHA where the sender had instructed BEN.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 generated with 71A BEN
→ A downstream bank copy shows 71A SHA
→ Charges split between sender and beneficiary instead of falling on the beneficiary
→ Sender billed for charges it never agreed to bear
→ Reconciliation breaks, nobody can agree who owes what

The requirement said:
"Copy the charge code from the previous bank's message."

So the code was retyped at every step instead of carried forward.

Why?

Field 71A is set by the bank that generates the MT103 and cannot be changed by later banks. Later banks can only add a field 71F when they take a charge. A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy worth querying, because the two codes give the beneficiary a different amount.

The charges equation always holds: field 32A equals field 33B plus field 71G minus all the 71F charges. Field 32A is the amount that settles between banks, field 33B is the amount the ordering customer instructed, field 71G is the receiver's charges prepaid by the sender, and field 71F is each sender's charge deducted along the way. If the equation does not balance, the code or a deduction is wrong.

71A is set once, by the bank that generates the MT103. Nobody downstream may change it.

BA Takeaway

The charge code is set once and carried, never retyped.

Keep these controls separate:

→ 71A as generated, never changed downstream
→ Each 71F deduction as it happens
→ The 32A reconciliation equation

The real requirement is not "What does our copy of the code say?"

It is "What evidence proves the charge code matches the original MT103?"

Have you ever found a charge code that changed hands mid-chain?

explain:
A payment of USD 75,000 to an overseas supplier passed sanctions screening and was released. The supplier was never paid. The funds were sitting in a hold at an intermediary bank.

Only one leg of the payment had been screened.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 screened, no hit, released
→ MT202 COV sent through the correspondent chain
→ Cover leg hits a sanctions list at an intermediary
→ Cover held for screening, MT103 left waiting
→ Originator believes the payment cleared screening

The requirement said:
"Screen the MT103 before release. The cover follows the same instruction."

So the funds leg travelled unscreened until an intermediary stopped it.

Why?

An MT103 and its MT202 COV are both subject to sanction screening, and the screening must happen before the payment is credited to the beneficiary. The information leg and the funds leg are screened separately, and a hit on either leg stops the payment. A bank that screens only the MT103 and not the cover, or the reverse, leaves a gap that a regulator will find.

One clean leg does not clear a payment. Both legs must pass.

The two legs can also name different ordering parties, because the MT103 names the customer who instructed the payment while the MT202 COV names the bank moving the funds. Screening has to cover the parties on each leg as that leg names them.

BA Takeaway

Screen both legs, or the payment is not screened.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT103 screening
→ MT202 COV screening
→ Hold handling and customer communication

The real requirement is not "Did the MT103 pass screening?"

It is "What evidence proves both legs passed screening before we credited the beneficiary?"

Have you ever released a payment that was still held on a leg nobody checked?

explain:
A payment of USD 60,000 passed through a correspondent bank on its way to the beneficiary. The beneficiary was paid. The originator bank could not prove it.

Its reconciliation broke, because the thread linking the two legs had been cut.

Here is what happened:

→ pacs.008 sent with a UETR in field 121
→ Correspondent bank receives the incoming leg
→ Correspondent sends the outgoing leg onward
→ Field 121 changed on the outgoing leg
→ Originator cannot match the payment it sent with the payment that arrived

The requirement said:
"Each bank may set its own reference on the leg it sends."

So the correspondent replaced the reference instead of carrying it forward.

Why?

When a payment passes through a correspondent bank, that bank sees two payments: the incoming payment from the sender and the outgoing payment to the next bank. The two legs are linked by the unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, which travels unchanged from one message to the next and is carried in field 121 of block 3. No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent.

The UETR is the thread. Break it and the payment cannot be traced.

The same discipline applies in the MT world and the MX world. A pacs.008 is the ISO 20022 customer credit transfer, the equivalent of an MT103, and a pacs.009 is the financial institution transfer, the equivalent of an MT202. The names change, the legs stay the same.

BA Takeaway

The reference belongs to the payment, not to the bank handling it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UETR carried unchanged through every leg
→ Field 121 integrity check at each handover
→ Reconciliation by UETR, not by local reference

The real requirement is not "Did each bank send its leg?"

It is "What evidence proves the outgoing leg is the same payment as the incoming leg?"

Have you ever lost a payment in reconciliation because a reference changed hands?

explain:
A customer sent USD 30,000 to a supplier's US dollar account. The supplier received USD 29,700 and sent the invoice back unpaid.

USD 300 had vanished in two currency conversions that should never have happened.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent in USD to a USD account
→ Intermediary converts USD to EUR
→ Next bank converts EUR back to USD
→ Beneficiary credited USD 29,700
→ Supplier treats the invoice as unpaid

The requirement said:
"Each bank may settle in whatever currency suits its own books."

So intermediaries converted the payment twice and charged for both conversions.

Why?

The sender decides the currency of a transaction, and no intermediary may change it on the way. If the beneficiary's account is in a different currency, the conversion happens as a separate foreign exchange step, and the beneficiary is credited in the currency of the account. A payment sent in dollars to a dollar account that arrives short because an intermediary converted it twice has gone wrong, and the banks in the chain must be challenged on it.

No intermediary may change the currency. The sender decides it.

The same rule protects the cover leg. In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 can carry different currencies, and fields 52, 53 and 54 describe the chain of banks that will fund the payment, but the currency of each leg follows the correspondent account it settles in. It is never changed mid-chain by an intermediary.

BA Takeaway

Currency is set by the sender and carried, never converted in passing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Currency as instructed
→ Foreign exchange as a separate, agreed step
→ Shortfall challenge against the chain

The real requirement is not "What currency did each bank use?"

It is "What evidence proves the currency the sender chose reached the beneficiary unchanged?"

Have you ever seen a payment arrive short because somebody converted it on the way?
